lines: Airlock Command
A cryptographic governance platform
for the post-quantum migration.
Recorded against a live build
and a fictional customer estate.
Traffic your organisation encrypts today
can be recorded today.
It becomes readable later, once a quantum computer
can break RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography.
So data with a long secrecy requirement
is already exposed, though nothing has been broken yet.
The company here is Example Financial Group —
an invented bank with thirty-eight endpoints.
The console opens on posture: inventory, open fixes,
modelled exposure and crypto-agility.
And the deadlines are not hypothetical.
CNSA 2.0, NSM-10 and NIST guidance carry published dates.
Optimistic, median and conservative scenarios —
not one confident date.
Some target dates have already passed.
Others land in 2030 and 2033.
The platform models when a relevant quantum computer
becomes credible — and labels it as a model.
Discovery.
Everything downstream starts with what you actually run,
not what the documentation says you run.
Airlock Command scans TLS endpoints and records
what each one really negotiated.
Protocol version, cipher suite, key algorithm,
key size, and the certificate chain behind it.
Eight scan runs over five months, so the history
has shape rather than being one snapshot.
The inventory it builds.
Each endpoint becomes an asset with an owner, a team,
an environment and a data-confidentiality lifetime.
RSA 2048 and 3072. Elliptic curve P-256 and P-384.
One gateway already negotiating a hybrid key exchange.
Confidentiality lifetime is the field that matters most —
how long this data has to stay secret.
Ownership is what turns a cryptographic finding
into work a named team can be asked to do.
Exposure.
Harvest now, decrypt later. The question is not
whether an endpoint is weak today.
It is what an adversary could store today
and read after Q-Day.
So each asset is priced: what the traffic is worth,
how long it stays secret, the odds it is broken by then.
Exposure grouped by algorithm class.
RSA-2048 carries most of it.
The priority queue is ranked by modelled exposure,
not by a severity label.
Owner, environment, algorithm, probability broken,
data category, and how long it has been harvestable.
Then the exposure timeline.
It is a real three-dimensional chart. You can turn it.
Amber is traffic captured but still sealed.
Red is the same traffic, readable,
once the model's Q-Day wall is crossed.
Beside it, the probability ribbons: one curve per algorithm,
with the year each reaches a fifty per cent chance.
Every modelled figure carries a badge saying it is a model,
with the date, the sources and the assumptions.
Nothing here is presented as measurement
when it is an estimate.
Evidence.
Exposure is an argument.
Evidence is what an auditor actually reads.
The cryptographic bill of materials is generated
from the scans themselves, in CycloneDX 1.6.
Every protocol, certificate and algorithm found,
each with its quantum status.
Eighty-seven components in this estate.
Two of them are already post-quantum.
Downloadable as JSON or CSV, so it can leave
the product and still mean something.
Then the mapping to control frameworks.
It is honest: this estate scores badly, and it says so.
Evidence packs collect the control artefacts
with timestamps and a hash chain.
Action.
Finding cryptography is the easy part.
Changing it is the work.
Every fix moves through suggested, approved,
pull request, and verified closed.
Two are closed and verified against a later scan.
Seven are still open.
Open one and it carries the file,
the current configuration, and the proposed change.
Approve, reject, validate, open a pull request, mark merged —
every step is recorded against the asset.
Before you change a certificate authority,
you want to know what depends on it.
Blast radius: assets, repositories and fixes
in one graph you can interrogate.
Two roots and two issuing authorities sit
under thirty-eight leaf certificates here.
If that public root failed, fifty-five dependent nodes
would be affected, and the model prices it.
And a tripwire ladder: five canary keys at five strengths.
Each only breaks if that algorithm breaks.
So the first one to trip tells you
how far quantum capability has actually reached.
Governance.
For the board, one composite score —
with every weight shown.
Inventory coverage, open exposure reduction,
crypto-agility, blocker control.
Components with no evidence behind them are marked
not measured, rather than scored from nothing.
Regulatory exposure is listed by regime,
with the alignment state the evidence supports.
The executive view is the same view the engineers
work in. There is no second set of numbers.
If you are the security team buying this,
four things matter.
One: tenant isolation is enforced in the database,
not only in application code.
Row-level security, scoped per organisation,
with a cross-tenant probe you can run yourself.
Two: vendor support cannot look at your workspace silently.
Read-only, time-limited, with a stated reason.
Three: the audit trail is hash-chained,
so a removed entry is detectable.
Four: the operators who run the platform sign in
through an identity provider, with authenticator MFA.
Destructive actions ask for a fresh code.
The shared key is an emergency credential only.
And the data boundary is explicit about what
is allowed to leave your environment.
Cryptographic metadata, fingerprints and workflow records
may cross. Source code, private keys and tokens do not.
Where to start.
A first pilot is deliberately narrow.
Six to eight weeks. One organisation.
Three to five critical applications,
and the assets that support them.
One approved cryptographic inventory.
One fix carried all the way to verified closure.
One evidence pack an auditor can read.
Start with the endpoints whose data
has to stay secret the longest.
Airlock Command.
Cryptographic governance for the post-quantum migration.
